title: SQL vs NoSQL
description: Evaluating relational databases against document, key-value and wide-column stores for a specific workload.
question: Which database should I choose: relational or NoSQL?
problems: should I use SQL or NoSQL
my database is becoming a bottleneck

sections.overview: Relational databases store data in tables with schemas, joins and ACID transactions. NoSQL is a broad family: document stores (MongoDB), key-value and wide-column stores (DynamoDB, Cassandra), each optimized for particular access patterns and horizontal scale.
sections.context: The useful question is not SQL or NoSQL in general, but which data model and consistency guarantees fit your queries. Relational databases are flexible for unknown future queries. NoSQL databases are fast and scalable for access patterns you design up front.
assumptions: You can describe your main read and write access patterns.
You know which operations need multi-record transactions.
whenToUse: Relational: evolving queries, joins, multi-entity transactions, reporting, strong constraints.
Key-value/wide-column: very high scale with known access patterns, predictable single-digit-millisecond lookups.
Document: self-contained aggregates read and written together, flexible schemas.
whenNotToUse: NoSQL when you need ad-hoc queries and joins across entities.
Relational when write volume or data size exceeds what one primary (plus replicas) can handle and the data shards poorly.
alternatives: Distributed SQL (CockroachDB, Spanner, YugabyteDB) for SQL semantics at horizontal scale.
Relational plus cache or search index for specific hot paths.
sections.operations: Managed offerings dominate both camps. Relational operations focus on vacuum/indexing, replicas and failover. NoSQL operations focus on partition key design, hot partitions and capacity modes.
sections.summary: Default to a relational database unless you have a known access pattern at a scale or latency that relational systems cannot meet, or your data is naturally document-shaped.

values: Vertical plus read replicas; sharding is hard

title: PostgreSQL vs MySQL
description: Comparing the two most widely used open-source relational databases for specific workloads.
question: Should we use PostgreSQL or MySQL?

sections.overview: Both are mature, well-supported relational databases available as managed services on every major cloud. PostgreSQL emphasizes standards compliance, extensibility and rich data types. MySQL (InnoDB) emphasizes simplicity, read performance and a long history of large-scale web use.
whenToUse: PostgreSQL: complex queries, JSONB, geospatial (PostGIS), extensions, strict SQL behaviour.
MySQL: simple high-volume OLTP, existing MySQL expertise, ecosystems built around it (e.g. Vitess for sharding).
whenNotToUse: Neither is wrong for typical web applications; team experience usually matters more than feature differences.
sections.operations: PostgreSQL requires attention to vacuum and connection management (connection poolers are common). MySQL replication and its sharding ecosystem are very mature.
sections.summary: Pick the one your team operates well. Prefer PostgreSQL for feature-rich data needs, MySQL where its scaling ecosystem or existing expertise matters.

title: Single Primary vs Multi Primary
description: Whether all writes go through one primary node or several nodes accept writes concurrently.
question: Do we need writes accepted in more than one place?

sections.overview: In single-primary replication, one node accepts writes and replicates them to followers. In multi-primary replication, several nodes accept writes and must resolve conflicting updates.
sections.context: Multi-primary is usually motivated by multi-region write latency or availability. It brings conflict resolution, which is a hard application-level problem.
whenToUse: Single primary: nearly all applications, including most multi-region read setups.
Multi primary: writes must succeed in several regions with low latency, and the data model tolerates conflict resolution (or a distributed SQL database handles consensus).
whenNotToUse: Multi primary for data with invariants that must hold globally (balances, unique reservations) unless you use a consensus-based database.
alternatives: Single primary with fast automated failover.
Partition data by region so each region has its own primary.
failureModes: Silent data loss from last-write-wins conflict resolution.
Split-brain during failover in single-primary setups without fencing.
Failover promoting a lagging replica and discarding writes.
sections.summary: Stay single-primary and invest in failover until write latency across regions is a proven business problem.

values: No single write node; conflicts instead
Remote writes travel to the primary

chooseWhen: Proven need for local writes in many regions

relations.note: Without automated failover, the primary is a single point of failure.
GitHub's 2018 incident involved cross-site MySQL failover.
Database topology constrains multi-region strategy.
Single-primary systems scale reads with replicas.

title: PostgreSQL
description: An extensible open-source relational database with strong SQL compliance and rich data types.

sections.overview: PostgreSQL provides ACID transactions with MVCC, rich types (JSONB, arrays, ranges), extensions (PostGIS, pgvector) and streaming replication.
sections.context: The default system of record for many applications. Managed offerings include Amazon RDS and Aurora, Google Cloud SQL and AlloyDB, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL.
whenToUse: General-purpose OLTP.
Mixed relational and JSON data.
Geospatial and vector search via extensions.
whenNotToUse: Process-per-connection model needs a pooler at high connection counts.
Write scaling beyond one primary requires sharding.
sections.summary: A strong default system of record.

relations.note: The other main open-source relational database.
Streaming replication feeds read replicas.
pgvector adds vector search.

title: MySQL
description: A widely deployed open-source relational database known for simple, high-volume OLTP.

sections.overview: MySQL with the InnoDB engine provides ACID transactions, mature replication and broad tooling. Large web companies have run it at very high scale, often with sharding layers such as Vitess.
whenToUse: High-volume web OLTP.
Teams with MySQL expertise.
whenNotToUse: Fewer advanced data types and extensions than PostgreSQL.
sections.summary: A proven choice for web-scale OLTP.

relations.note: Vitess and similar layers shard MySQL.
GitHub runs MySQL at large scale.

title: Amazon DynamoDB
description: AWS's fully managed key-value and document database with predictable latency at any scale.

sections.overview: DynamoDB stores items by partition key (and optional sort key), scales horizontally, and offers on-demand or provisioned capacity with no servers to manage.
whenToUse: Known access patterns at large scale.
Serverless architectures with Lambda.
whenNotToUse: Ad-hoc queries and joins.
Poor partition key choice creates hot partitions.
sections.summary: Excellent when you design access patterns first.

relations.note: Trades query flexibility for managed horizontal scale.
A common serverless pairing.

title: Read Replicas
description: Copies of a primary database that serve read traffic, trading freshness for read capacity.
problems: how do I reduce database load
my database is becoming a bottleneck

sections.overview: Replicas receive changes from the primary asynchronously (usually) and serve read queries. They scale reads and can be promoted during failover.
whenToUse: Read-heavy workloads.
Reporting queries that should not load the primary.
whenNotToUse: Write-bound workloads.
Reads that must see the latest write, unless routed to the primary.
failureModes: Replication lag causing users to not see their own writes.
Replica overload when the primary fails over and capacity shrinks.
implementation: Route read-your-writes paths to the primary.
Monitor lag and remove lagging replicas from rotation.
sections.summary: The standard first step for read scaling in relational databases.

relations.note: When writes, not reads, are the bottleneck.
Replicas are eventually consistent.

title: Sharding
description: Partitioning data across multiple databases by a shard key to scale writes and storage.

sections.overview: Sharding splits a dataset into shards, each on its own database, according to a shard key (tenant, user, region, hash). Each shard handles a fraction of writes and storage.
whenToUse: Write throughput or data size beyond one primary.
Natural partition keys such as tenant ID.
whenNotToUse: Before exhausting vertical scaling, query optimization, caching and replicas.
Workloads dominated by cross-entity queries.
failureModes: Cross-shard transactions and queries becoming expensive.
Resharding operations that are risky and slow.
sections.summary: Powerful and hard to undo; choose the shard key carefully and late.

relations.note: Sharding too early or too finely.
Moving to a horizontally scalable database is the alternative to sharding a relational one.

title: Database per Service
description: Each service owns its data store; others access the data only through the service's API or events.

sections.overview: Each microservice has a private database. No other service reads its tables directly. This keeps services independently deployable.
whenToUse: Microservices that must evolve schemas independently.
whenNotToUse: Modular monoliths can use one database with schema-per-module instead.
failureModes: Distributed transactions and inconsistency across services.
Reporting that needs data from many services.
implementation: Use events or an outbox to share changes.
Build a separate analytics store for cross-service reporting.
sections.summary: Essential for real microservice independence; brings data consistency work.

relations.note: Services share state changes through events.
Cross-service data is eventually consistent.

title: Event Sourcing
description: Storing state as an append-only sequence of events and deriving current state by replaying them.

sections.overview: Instead of updating rows, the system records every change as an event. Current state is a projection built from the event log. Often combined with CQRS (separate read models).
whenToUse: Domains where history and auditability are core (ledgers, compliance).
When many read models must be derived from the same changes.
whenNotToUse: Typical CRUD applications.
Teams new to eventual consistency.
sections.summary: Valuable in history-centric domains; costly elsewhere.

relations.note: Events are the primary data structure.
Sometimes used as the event log transport.
Applied to simple domains, it adds machinery with little benefit.

title: Amazon S3 vs Cloudflare R2
description: Comparing AWS's object storage with Cloudflare's S3-compatible storage that does not charge egress fees.
question: Should we store objects in S3 or R2?

sections.overview: S3 is the reference object store with many storage classes, lifecycle policies and deep AWS integration. R2 offers an S3-compatible API with no egress charges, positioned for content served to the internet.
whenToUse: S3: data processed inside AWS, need for storage classes and archival tiers, event integrations.
R2: egress-heavy public content, multi-cloud access, Cloudflare Workers integration.
whenNotToUse: S3 for egress-heavy public delivery without a CDN.
R2 when workloads depend on S3-specific features or AWS-native integrations.
sections.cost: Pricing changes; check current pages. The structural difference is egress: S3 charges for data transfer out to the internet, R2 does not.
sections.summary: Keep data near the compute that processes it. Use R2 or a CDN when internet egress dominates cost.

relations.note: One option.
The other option.
Egress cost per user is a unit economics question.

title: Amazon S3
description: AWS's highly durable object storage service with multiple storage classes and lifecycle management.

sections.overview: S3 stores objects in buckets, designed for very high durability, with storage classes from frequent access to deep archive and lifecycle rules to move data between them.
whenToUse: Backups, data lakes, media, static assets, logs.
whenNotToUse: Low-latency random block access (use block storage).
POSIX file semantics (use file storage).
sections.summary: The default object store on AWS.

relations.note: S3-compatible alternative without egress fees.
Misconfigured access policies expose data publicly.

title: Cloudflare R2
description: S3-compatible object storage from Cloudflare with no egress fees.

sections.overview: R2 exposes an S3-compatible API, integrates with Cloudflare Workers, and does not bill for egress.
whenToUse: Public assets and downloads with high egress.
whenNotToUse: Workloads requiring S3-only features or tight AWS integration.
sections.summary: A cost lever for egress-heavy storage.

relations.note: Part of Cloudflare's developer platform.
